cases.title: Puerto Varas case: from rural restriction to commercial vocation | Land Advisors
cases.description: Real case in Puerto Varas: land with commercial use prohibition, territorial reading of connectivity and urban expansion, and estimated capture of +50% on purchase price.
cases.h1: From rural restriction to commercial vocation
cases.intro: A commercial piece of land on the Puerto Varas fringe carried an explicit commercial use prohibition in the listing. The market ruled it out; territorial reading told a different story.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Puerto Varas and Lago Llanquihue surroundings

ila.thesisMarket: The commercial use prohibition in the listing closed the conversation for the market.
ila.thesisTerritory: Connectivity, adjacent urbanisation and corridor trajectory suggested a commercial vocation different from what the listing conveyed.

sections.text: Problem

The buyer wanted land with commercial vocation on the peri-urban fringe of Puerto Varas. The listing showed an attractive location, but the documentation included an explicit commercial use restriction. For most interested parties, that closed the conversation.
Territorial analysis

We reviewed real connectivity (not just map distance), vehicle flow on the corridor, urban expansion trajectory in the sector and the property's regulatory background. The restriction existed on paper, but the territorial context — access improvements, adjacent urbanisation and municipal investment on the fringe — suggested a commercial vocation different from what the listing conveyed.

items: Connectivity and real travel times to urban services
Planning instruments applicable to the property
Local comparables for land with similar vocation

sections.text: Decision

With verifiable information, the buyer proceeded understanding the regulatory risk and the scenario for lifting the restriction. The decision was not based on the land photo: it was based on the relationship between entry price, territorial vocation and negotiation margin.
Outcome
After the corresponding process, the commercial use prohibition was lifted. Estimated value capture was approximately 50% above the purchase price.
Transferable learning

A restriction in the listing does not always close the opportunity — but it does require regulatory and territorial reading before making an offer. The reverse is also true: land that appears 'free' on paper can be expensive if enabling costs or connectivity do not support it.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalised advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Can a commercial use restriction always be lifted?
faq.a: No. It depends on the property, the current planning instrument and the applicable procedure. Each case requires regulatory verification before assuming a lifting scenario.

faq.q: Why did the market rule out this land?
faq.a: The visible prohibition in the listing acts as an automatic filter. Without reading connectivity, urban expansion and local comparables, many buyers never reach a full territorial assessment.

faq.q: Did Land Advisors sell this land?
faq.a: No. We are territorial consultancy: we support the purchase decision with market and territory criteria. We are not an estate agency or property portal.

cases.title: Frutillar case: the opportunity was in the seller | Land Advisors
cases.description: Real case in Frutillar: gap between asking price and real value, seller urgency and arbitrage from 26M to 42M in two months.
cases.h1: The opportunity was in the seller
cases.intro: For the market it was another piece of land in the Frutillar supply. For someone reading liquidity and comparables, it was an actionable price gap.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Land in Frutillar, Lago Llanquihue basin

ila.thesisMarket: For the market it was another piece of land in the visible Frutillar supply.
ila.thesisTerritory: The gap was in seller liquidity and local comparables — not in future sector capital growth.

sections.text: Problem
The buyer was evaluating alternatives in Frutillar within a defined budget. The visible supply included dozens of similar listings — hard to compare without local criteria.
Territorial analysis

We contrasted the asking price with real sales in the area (not just active listings), reviewed the sector vocation within the Frutillar rural fringe and detected seller urgency signals: need for liquidity and a tight timeline.
Decision
The purchase was structured on the verifiable gap between list price and local market value, not on a future capital growth narrative. The return was in the transaction itself.
Outcome
Purchase at 26 million pesos and resale at 42 million in approximately two months, with comparables supporting the exit value.
Transferable learning

Not all returns depend on waiting years for a sector to transform. Sometimes the return is in buying well — identifying price gaps, seller liquidity and pricing errors — with local comparables to back it up.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalised advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Does this type of arbitrage repeat in Frutillar?
faq.a: Price gaps appear when there is information asymmetry or seller urgency. They are not replicable on demand: each opportunity requires local market reading and verifiable comparables.

faq.q: How do you distinguish a low price from problematic land?
faq.a: A low price can be opportunity or a risk signal (access, services, regulation). The difference lies in contrasting purchase price, enabling costs and exit value with local data.

faq.q: Which service fits if I am looking for this type of opportunity?
faq.a: Personalised search filters at least 4 alternatives with territorial criteria; the session with you defines the 3 best to compare in a report.

cases.title: Llanquihue case: present value vs. future value | Land Advisors
cases.description: Real case in Llanquihue: partly urbanised project, developer liquidity shortfall and purchase of 4 plots of land for 4,400 UF with later reference ~2,000 UF per plot.
cases.intro: A partly urbanised development can look attractive on unit price. The right question is whether present value compensates for enabling risk and timelines.
cases.author: José Hernán Katz C.
cases.imageAlt: Rural sector in Llanquihue with development potential

ila.thesisMarket: The price per plot looked competitive against standalone alternatives.
ila.thesisTerritory: The opportunity was in present value negotiated with developer liquidity — not in a distant capital growth promise.

sections.text: Problem

The buyer was evaluating a partly urbanised development in Llanquihue. The price per plot looked competitive against standalone alternatives, but there was no contrast with pending enabling costs, real timelines and exit liquidity.
Territorial analysis

We reviewed urbanisation status, effective vs. promised services, subdivision regulation, post-enabling comparables in the sector and — critically — the developer's liquidity situation, which conditioned the negotiation.

items: Comparables for enabled land in the area

sections.text: Decision
The purchase was structured on verifiable present value: negotiated entry price in a context of seller liquidity, with a conservative post-urbanisation value projection — not on project promises.
Outcome
Acquisition of 4 plots for 4,400 UF in total. Subsequent market reference: approximately 2,000 UF per enabled plot under comparable conditions.
Transferable learning

In partly urbanised projects, the 'per plot' price can hide pending costs and timelines. Add purchase price + enabling + time, and compare with a conservative sale scenario — not with the developer brochure.
Past results do not guarantee future results. Illustrative case with aggregated data. Does not constitute personalised advice or a promise of returns.

faq.q: Is it worth buying in a partly urbanised subdivision?
faq.a: It can be if present value closes with verifiable comparables and pending costs are quantified. If the price already incorporates future value without support, risk rises.

faq.q: What should I review in the co-ownership bylaws?
faq.a: Permitted uses, construction restrictions, pending urbanisation fees and administration rules. In subdivisions, this can limit cabins, retail or density.

faq.q: Does Land Advisors recommend specific projects?
faq.a: We do not sell land or projects. We evaluate alternatives against your objective and recommend with data — including telling you when to keep searching.
